questions.q: State what is meant by defensive design.

markPoints.concept: writing a program so that it copes with being used wrongly
markPoints.exemplar: Writing a program so that it anticipates being used wrongly.

questions.example: Writing a program so that it anticipates the mistakes and misuse it will meet, and copes with them rather than crashing.
questions.paraphrase: Designing code that expects users to do unexpected things and handles it.
questions.feedback: Anticipating misuse. A program that only works when everything goes right has not been designed defensively.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: Which of these are part of designing a program defensively? Tick all that apply.
options: Validating every input before using it
Checking that a file exists before opening it
Giving a helpful message when something goes wrong
Requiring users to authenticate before reaching private data
Writing the program in as few lines as possible
Making the program run as fast as possible
correct: Validating every input before using it
Checking that a file exists before opening it
Giving a helpful message when something goes wrong
Requiring users to authenticate before reaching private data
questions.feedback: Speed and brevity are not defences. A short fast program that crashes on bad input is not robust.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: Explain why a program should check that a file exists before trying to open it.

markPoints.concept: opening a file that is not there causes an error
markPoints.exemplar: Trying to open a file that is not there causes an error.

markPoints.concept: so the program can give a sensible message instead of stopping
markPoints.exemplar: Checking first means that the program can tell the user instead of crashing.

questions.example: If the file is missing, trying to open it raises an error and the program stops. Checking first lets it tell the user that the file could not be found and carry on, which is far better than crashing in front of them.
questions.paraphrase: Attempting to open a non-existent file throws an error that halts the program, so testing for it first allows a sensible message to be shown and execution to continue.
questions.feedback: What goes wrong, and what checking lets you do instead.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.3 Lesson 2 — Cyber defence HQ, station 1: Anticipating misuse

questions.q: A website asks a user to type a word shown in a distorted image. What is this for?
options: To check that the user is a person rather than an automated program
To check that the user's keyboard works
To encrypt the user's password before sending it
To validate the format of the user's email address
questions.feedback: A CAPTCHA defends against bots submitting the form thousands of times.
